--- title: "Decision trees" description: "A decision tree predicts by asking yes-or-no questions about the inputs. It can be read like an identification key, predicts in steps that stay level beyond the data, and needs its depth chosen on held-back data." order: 5 categories: [supervised, trees-ensembles] --- ## A model made of questions Every model so far in this section weights the inputs and adds them up. A decision tree works differently: it asks a series of yes-or-no questions about the inputs, such as whether the water is colder than 6 °C, and predicts from the answers. Nobody writes down the shape of the relationship; the questions find it. [Statistical modelling and machine learning](../01-introduction/what-is-machine-learning.qmd) fitted one to three inputs. This page shows how a tree is grown, how to read one, and how deep to let it grow. The random forests and boosting on the [next page](forests-and-boosting.qmd) are built from many trees. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. Both run when the site is built, and each tab shows its own output. The Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent of the R; the figures come from R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly** where randomness is involved: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## Growing a tree one question at a time A tree starts with all the training data together. Its first question splits them in two on one input: every example below a threshold goes one way, every example above it the other. Each half is then split again with its own question, and so on. A group that is split no further is a **leaf**, and its prediction is the average outcome of the training examples in it. For a category, a leaf gives the share of each category instead, which serves as a probability, so the same method does classification. To choose each question, the algorithm tries every input and every threshold and keeps the split that brings the predictions closest to the training data: for a quantity, the smallest total of squared errors. It then moves on and never revisits a choice. The tree stops growing when it reaches a set **depth**, the number of questions from the top to a leaf, or when a group is too small to split. ::: {.diagram} ![A decision tree asks yes-or-no questions; each leaf predicts the average of the examples that reach it. The questions cut the inputs into boxes, and the prediction changes in steps that stay level beyond the data.](img/decision-tree.svg){fig-alt="Three cards. Questions, a tree of yes-or-no questions: the first asks whether input 1 is below 6; if yes, a leaf predicts 2.1; if no, a second question asks whether input 2 is below 10, with leaves predicting 5.2 and 2.6. Each leaf predicts the average of the examples that reach it. Boxes, the questions cut up the inputs: a square of input 1 against input 2 is cut by a vertical line at 6, and its right part by a horizontal line at 10, giving three boxes labelled 2.1, 5.2 and 2.6; every example in a box gets the same prediction. Steps, flat beyond the data: the prediction against one input is a staircase, low, then high, then middle, and it stays level in the shaded regions beyond the data at either end. A note says a deeper tree asks more questions and fits its training data more closely, noise included."} ::: ## Deeper trees fit more closely Each extra level of questions cuts the data into smaller groups, so the leaves follow the training data more closely. Grown until every leaf holds a single example, a tree reproduces its training data exactly, including the chance ups and downs that will not recur, and predicts new data badly. Fitting the training data so closely that predictions on new data get worse is **overfitting**, and [Underfitting and overfitting](../05-generalisation/underfitting-and-overfitting.qmd) covers it in full. The depth is therefore chosen on validation data, the role [Splitting the data](../02-marine-data/splitting-data.qmd) set aside for choosing between models. ## Worked example The data and the split by site are those of the earlier pages. A tree needs no squared terms, since its questions can find a peak, and no dummy columns: rpart, the package tidymodels uses for trees, asks questions about a category directly, such as whether the seabed is mud or rock. The recipe only fills the gaps. The training stations are split once more by site, into fitting and validation sites, for choosing the depth later. ### Preparing the data ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() split <- group_initial_split(survey, group = site_id, prop = 0.75) train <- training(split) test <- testing(split) fit_split <- group_initial_split(train, group = site_id, prop = 0.75) fitting <- training(fit_split) validation <- testing(fit_split) predictors <- abundance ~ depth_m + temperature_c + chlorophyll_mg_m3 + salinity_psu + substrate + season tree_recipe <- recipe(predictors, data = train) |> step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) ``` ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer from sklearn.metrics import root_mean_squared_error from sklearn.model_selection import GroupShuffleSplit from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor, export_text from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean survey = load_coastal_survey_clean() numeric = ["depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu"] categorical = ["substrate", "season"] predictors = numeric + categorical grouper = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, train_size=0.75, random_state=123) train_rows, test_rows = next(grouper.split(survey, groups=survey["site_id"])) train, test = survey.iloc[train_rows], survey.iloc[test_rows] inner = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, train_size=0.75, random_state=123) fit_rows, val_rows = next(inner.split(train, groups=train["site_id"])) fitting, validation = train.iloc[fit_rows], train.iloc[val_rows] # scikit-learn's trees need numbers, so each category becomes 0/1 columns. tree_recipe = ColumnTransformer([ ("numeric", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), numeric), ("categorical", OneHotEncoder(sparse_output=False), categorical), ], verbose_feature_names_out=False) ``` ::: ::: ### A tree you can read `decision_tree()` sets the depth. rpart normally also stops at a split that improves the fit only a little; `cost_complexity = 0` turns that off, and `min_n = 2` lets it split any group of two or more, so the depth alone sets the size of the tree. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tree_model <- function(depth) { decision_tree(mode = "regression", tree_depth = depth, min_n = 2, cost_complexity = 0) } tree_fit <- workflow(tree_recipe, tree_model(3)) |> fit(train) ``` ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} def tree_model(depth, data): model = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=depth, random_state=123) return Pipeline([("recipe", tree_recipe), ("model", model)]).fit( data[predictors], data["abundance"]) tree_fit = tree_model(3, train) print(export_text(tree_fit["model"], decimals=1, feature_names=list(tree_fit["recipe"].get_feature_names_out()))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> |--- chlorophyll_mg_m3 <= 9.5 #> | |--- chlorophyll_mg_m3 <= 1.3 #> | | |--- temperature_c <= 5.9 #> | | | |--- value: [1.3] #> | | |--- temperature_c > 5.9 #> | | | |--- value: [3.3] #> | |--- chlorophyll_mg_m3 > 1.3 #> | | |--- chlorophyll_mg_m3 <= 5.7 #> | | | |--- value: [5.1] #> | | |--- chlorophyll_mg_m3 > 5.7 #> | | | |--- value: [11.5] #> |--- chlorophyll_mg_m3 > 9.5 #> | |--- value: [37.0] ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rpart.plot(tree_engine, roundint = FALSE, type = 2, extra = 101, box.palette = "Blues", branch.lty = 3, cex = 0.8) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The depth-3 tree for the count. Each box shows the average count of the training stations that reach it, how many stations that is, and their share of all training stations. Follow the answer yes to the left and no to the right.](decision-trees_files/figure-html/fig-tree-1.png){#fig-tree fig-alt='A decision tree three questions deep. The first question asks whether chlorophyll is below 5.7; the 15 stations above it average 15.9 animals. The rest are split on temperature at 6.4 and 10.4 degrees, giving leaves for cold, middle and warm water, with the most animals in the middle.' width=1800} ::: ::: Read it from the top. The first question sets apart the 15 training stations with more than 5.7 mg m⁻³ of chlorophyll, which average 15.9 animals against 3.7 for the rest. Squared errors weigh large counts heavily, so a question that sets apart a few stations with many animals can reduce them more than any other. The remaining stations are split twice on temperature. Below 6.4 °C they average 1.5 animals, above 10.4 °C 2.6, and in between 5.2, across 304 stations. The tree has found a temperature band with the most animals, and it took two questions to do it: one threshold can only say "more above" or "more below", so a peak needs one question for each side. A short tree can be printed and read like an identification key, which makes it easy to explain to someone who does not model. The thresholds are where this sample happened to split best, though, not values with a biological meaning; the first exercise below shows how much they move. ### Predictions come in steps @fig-steps sets the tree beside the Poisson curve of [Regression for counts](count-regression.qmd), fitted to the same training stations, across a wider range of temperatures than the survey sampled. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} grid <- tibble( temperature_c = seq(0, 20, length.out = 400), depth_m = median(train$depth_m, na.rm = TRUE), chlorophyll_mg_m3 = median(train$chlorophyll_mg_m3, na.rm = TRUE), salinity_psu = median(train$salinity_psu, na.rm = TRUE), substrate = factor("sand", levels = levels(train$substrate)), season = factor("summer", levels = levels(train$season)) ) curves <- bind_rows( augment(tree_fit, grid) |> mutate(model = "Decision tree"), augment(poisson_fit, grid) |> mutate(model = "Poisson curve") ) ggplot(curves, aes(temperature_c, .pred, colour = model)) + annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = temp_range[1], ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = ml_palette[["grey"]], alpha = 0.12) + annotate("rect", xmin = temp_range[2], xmax = Inf, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = ml_palette[["grey"]], alpha = 0.12) + geom_rug(data = train, aes(temperature_c), inherit.aes = FALSE, sides = "b", alpha = 0.3, colour = ml_palette[["grey"]]) + geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) + scale_colour_manual(values = c("Decision tree" = ml_palette[["green"]], "Poisson curve" = ml_palette[["vermilion"]])) + labs(x = "Temperature (°C)", y = "Predicted count", colour = NULL, title = "The tree predicts in steps and stays level beyond the data") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The predicted count across temperature, with the other inputs held at their typical values (sand, summer, median depth, chlorophyll and salinity). The shaded ends lie beyond the temperatures of the training stations, shown as ticks along the bottom.](decision-trees_files/figure-html/fig-steps-1.png){#fig-steps fig-alt='Two lines of predicted count against temperature from 0 to 20 degrees. The tree is a staircase: low in cold water, a step up to its highest level in the middle of the range, and a step down in warm water, after which it stays level through the shaded region beyond the warmest training station. The Poisson curve rises smoothly to a peak in the same middle range and falls towards zero on both sides, continuing to fall in the shaded regions.' width=1500} ::: ::: Both models find the most animals in the middle of the range, but the tree gets there in steps: every station on the same side of each threshold gets the same prediction, however far it is from the threshold. Beyond the warmest training station, at 16 °C, the tree keeps predicting what it predicted for the warmest stations it saw. It has no rule for going further, so it predicts no change. The Poisson curve continues its shape instead. Neither has any data there, and [Section 6](../06-assumptions-limitations/index.qmd) returns to predicting beyond the data. ### Choosing the depth Trees of each depth from 1 to 15 are fitted on the fitting sites, three quarters of the training sites, and scored on the validation sites, the rest. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} score_depth <- function(depth) { fitted <- workflow(tree_recipe, tree_model(depth)) |> fit(fitting) error <- function(data) { rmse_vec(data$abundance, predict(fitted, data)$.pred) } tibble(depth = depth, training = error(fitting), validation = error(validation)) } depths <- map(1:15, score_depth) |> list_rbind() depths |> slice_min(validation) |> mutate(across(-depth, \(x) round(x, 2))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| depth| training| validation| |-----:|--------:|----------:| | 5| 3.77| 3.63|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} def rmse(fitted, data): return root_mean_squared_error(data["abundance"], fitted.predict(data[predictors])) rows = [] for depth in range(1, 16): fitted = tree_model(depth, fitting) rows.append({"depth": depth, "training": rmse(fitted, fitting), "validation": rmse(fitted, validation)}) depths = pd.DataFrame(rows) depths.loc[[depths["validation"].idxmin()]].round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | depth | training | validation | |--------:|-----------:|-------------:| | 5 | 3.2 | 4.7 | ::: ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} best_depth <- depths |> slice_min(validation) |> pull(depth) depths |> pivot_longer(c(training, validation), names_to = "data", values_to = "rmse") |> ggplot(aes(depth, rmse, colour = data)) + geom_vline(xintercept = best_depth, linetype = "dashed", colour = ml_palette[["grey"]]) + geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) + geom_point(size = 2) + scale_colour_manual(values = c(training = ml_palette[["blue"]], validation = ml_palette[["orange"]])) + scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1, 15, 2)) + expand_limits(y = 0) + labs(x = "Tree depth", y = "RMSE", colour = NULL, title = "Deeper trees fit their own stations better, new sites worse") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The RMSE of trees of each depth on the stations they were fitted to and on the validation sites. The dashed line marks the depth with the lowest validation error.](decision-trees_files/figure-html/fig-depth-1.png){#fig-depth fig-alt='Two lines of RMSE against tree depth from 1 to 15. The training line falls steadily, close to zero at depth 15. The validation line falls a little over the first few depths, reaches its lowest point at a middle depth marked by a dashed line, then rises well above where it started.' width=1400} ::: ::: The training error falls with every level, from 4.82 at depth 1 to 0.55 at depth 15, where the tree nearly reproduces the counts it was fitted to. The validation error falls only from 3.93 to 3.63 at depth 5, then climbs to 4.94: past that depth, the extra questions fit chance patterns in the fitting sites. ### The chosen tree on new sites The tree is refitted at depth 5 on all the training stations and scored once on the test sites. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} final_fit <- workflow(tree_recipe, tree_model(best_depth)) |> fit(train) predicted <- predict(final_fit, test)$.pred tibble(rmse = round(rmse_vec(test$abundance, predicted), 2), rsq = round(rsq_vec(test$abundance, predicted), 2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| rmse| rsq| |----:|----:| | 4.48| 0.04|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} best_depth = int(depths.loc[depths["validation"].idxmin(), "depth"]) final_fit = tree_model(best_depth, train) predicted = final_fit.predict(test[predictors]) pd.DataFrame({ "rmse": [root_mean_squared_error(test["abundance"], predicted)], "rsq": [np.corrcoef(predicted, test["abundance"])[0, 1] ** 2], }).round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | rmse | rsq | |-------:|------:| | 5.7 | 0.17 | ::: ::: ::: On the test sites the tree's RMSE is 4.48, worse than its validation error of 3.63, and its $R^2$ is 0.04. The Poisson curve of [Regression for counts](count-regression.qmd) scored 3.55 and 0.24 on the same sites. Two things are at work. A few validation sites are a noisy guide to the best depth, and [Section 7](../07-validation/index.qmd) averages over several splits instead. And a single tree is unstable: a small change in the training data can change the first question, and everything below it changes too. The [next page](forests-and-boosting.qmd) averages many trees to steady them. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - A decision tree predicts by asking yes-or-no questions about the inputs; each leaf predicts the average outcome of the training examples in it, or for a category the share of each. - The tree is grown one question at a time, each the best available at that step, and a short tree can be read like an identification key. - A peak takes two questions, one for each side: the survey's tree found a band from 6.4 to 10.4 °C with the most animals. - Predictions change in steps and stay level beyond the data. - Deeper trees fit their training data ever more closely and new data worse, so the depth is chosen on validation data. The chosen tree predicted the test sites less well than the Poisson curve. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Change the seed before the split to 124 and refit the depth-3 tree. Which question comes first now, and how far do the temperature thresholds move? 2. Fit a depth-3 classification tree to `present` with `decision_tree(mode = "classification", tree_depth = 3)`. Which question comes first, and what share of the stations in each leaf are present?
